I grew up with the Star Wars prequels, and I like that, despite being a gazillionaire, he’s still rocking the same flannels he always has. The legendary filmmaker — fresh off a great cameo in the movie “Minions and Monsters” — is a big racing fan, and is often seen at Formula 1 races . He also binned a Scion during the old Toyota Pro/Celebrity Race at Long Beach in one of my favorite videos ever. So he knows racing — hell, he invented podracing — but F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali revealed a wild bit of advice he got from the man who somehow invented both Darth Vader and Jar-Jar Binks: no one is interested in how F1 cars are driven. I don’t think that’s true, but let’s hear him out. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The series has faced a lot of flak for its current cars that rely more heavily on battery power and have effectively changed how drivers have to drive. Certain iconic corners are no longer taken flat out, and the need to recharge batteries has led to people calling the racing artificial. It has also led to claims that F1 should offer more info about the batteries and their state of charge for fans to follow along. “I think that the truth is exactly the other way around, because no one is interested in how you drive your car,” Domenicali said, per Motorsport . “The people are interested in whether you are overtaking or not. That’s the vast majority of people.” He noted that while some people are interested in this sort of thing, casual fans aren’t. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Then he delivered one of the greatest name drops I’ve ever read. “I had an interesting discussion with George Lucas in Hungary, and he was giving me an incredible view on how the new fans are watching F1,” Domenicali said. “And I think that he gave us an incredible clearance to see how we can really simplify things because the new fans are not understanding the truth, what is behind the scenes.” I think new fans appreciate the sport more once they get a firmer grasp on the behind-the-scenes stuff, but it’s interesting Lucas made this point because it sounds to me like he’s saying what’s most important is providing an entertaining product. He knows quite a bit about that. Hell, he just opened a massive museum devoted to the medium of storytelling. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS And, if you think about it, every race is one big story, and it makes sense that F1 would want that at the forefront for newer fans. But, if you’re already in the door, there’s always room to nerd out on the strategies and tech and science behind the sport, just like if you’re a fan of a movie, you can geek out on the plot devices and the structure and even what pen or script software the person who wrote it used. It’s an interesting thing to think about… and even more fun because it seems to have sprung from the flannel-shirted mind of one George Lucas. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP Sydney ‘The engine’s on fire’: Qantas flight from Queenstown to Sydney reroutes after flames seen by passengers Passenger recalls seeing cabin lights flicker and ‘a lot of screaming’ after suspected engine issue Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Sun 6 Sep 2026 03.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when her Qantas flight ran into trouble. The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island’s mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney , when a bang shook the cabin. A passenger seated near the left wing soon shouted “the engine’s on fire”, Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker. Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane’s left engine in a series of rapid bursts. “I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible,” Loch said. “There was a lot of screaming at the time.” As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “That’s what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine,” she said. “But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming.” Qantas flight QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch. According to FlightAware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after takeoff, touching down shortly before 5pm local time. The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate. Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight. Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff sought to comfort passengers. “The crew were all terribly, terribly calming,” Loch said. Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, with passengers allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait. “There were massive cheers when we landed,” Loch said. A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers. “Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely,” they said. “We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support.” Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch international airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday. While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high. “I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney,” Loch said. “It was quite traumatic.” Explore more on these topics Sydney Queenstown New Zealand Qantas Airline industry Transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
